idiom_name: scala-rules: Glossary of Facts + Derivations evaluated into a Context
implementation_notes: scala-rules models the rule base as Facts (name plus type) declared in a Glossary and Derivations that combine them; the DSL reads Gegeven(condition) Bereken fact is expression, and the engine repeatedly applies derivations, storing results in a Context until nothing further can be derived. Input facts are supplied as a Context map and the engine returns the enriched context, while runDebugDerivations also reports the Steps that fired and why - an explainability story most engines only offer through logging. Rules are typed Scala values rather than a rule file, so they refactor with the code at the cost of requiring a build to change.
code_sketch:
import org.scalarules.dsl.nl.grammar._
import PricingGlossary._

class Pricing extends Berekening(
  Gegeven(orderUnits > 100 && loyaltyYears > 2) Bereken discountPercentage is 10,
  Gegeven(discountPercentage > 0) Bereken freeShipping is true
)

val context = Context(initialFacts = Map(orderUnits -> 250, loyaltyYears -> 5))
val (result, steps) = runDebugDerivations(context)   // steps: what fired and why
pitfalls: The Berekening constructor takes a comma-separated derivation list and silently receives an empty list if braces are used instead of parentheses - the engine then runs with no rules and no error.
A derivation must declare every fact it consumes: a missing input is only noticed when the engine cannot resolve the value, so glossaries need consistency tests.
Forward chaining continues while new facts can be derived: derivations that feed each other do not terminate, so the derivation graph must stay acyclic.

variants.name: Drools/KIE over Scala facts
variants.idiom_name: Drools/KIE with case classes annotated for JavaBean access
variants.implementation_notes: Because Scala runs on the JVM, Drools is available unchanged: rules live in .drl files, facts are Scala case classes, and the KieBase resolves property names through JavaBean getters - so fact classes need @BeanProperty fields (or @BeanInfo on the class) and dependable equals/hashCode, which case classes already provide. Consequences mutate facts via modify()/setX() and therefore require var properties where a rule updates them, and collections passed in bulk should be Java collections. Use a stateless session or one session per unit of work, and keep the .drl files under test because their class and property references are resolved at KieBase build time.
pitfalls: Without @BeanProperty (or @BeanInfo) Drools cannot see Scala properties: patterns then match nothing instead of failing, which reads like a wrong rule rather than a missing annotation.
Case-class vals expose getters but no setters, so DRL modify()/setX() consequences need a var field or a newly inserted fact.
Scala types are not JavaBean types: Option is not a property Drools can read, and Scala collections must be converted to java.util collections before insertion.
